bio11-classification.title: Biodiversity, classification and evolutionary relationships
bio11-classification.coverage: Lesson concept checks followed by related subject revision.

questions.prompt: Biodiversity, classification and evolutionary relationships — Two samples each contain four species but one is dominated by a single species. What differs?
questions.explanation: Evenness describes relative abundances; richness is four in both samples.

questions.prompt: Biodiversity, classification and evolutionary relationships — What best tests genetic diversity within a population?
options: Variation in inherited sequences or alleles
questions.explanation: Within-species genetic diversity requires evidence of inherited variation, not a species count alone.

questions.prompt: Biodiversity, classification and evolutionary relationships — Which rank lies between family and species in the common hierarchy?
questions.explanation: The sequence includes order, family, genus and species, with genus containing related species.

questions.prompt: Biodiversity, classification and evolutionary relationships — Which organisms most limit direct use of the biological species concept?
questions.explanation: The concept centres on natural reproductive compatibility, which cannot be directly tested in fossils or applied in the same way to asexual lineages.

questions.prompt: Biodiversity, classification and evolutionary relationships — How are sister tips recognised in a phylogenetic tree?
options: By the most recent shared node
questions.explanation: Topology and common ancestry determine inferred relationship; rotating a branch does not change it.

questions.prompt: Ecological fieldwork, data and scientific inquiry — For M=20,C=40,R=8, what is estimated population size?
questions.explanation: Capture–recapture uses M×C/R, so 20×40/8=100 under its assumptions.

questions.prompt: Habitats, ecological niches and species interactions — Why can predator abundance peak after prey abundance?
options: Predator reproduction responds with a delay
questions.explanation: Improved prey availability can increase predator survival/reproduction, but demographic responses take time.

questions.prompt: Population dynamics, carrying capacity, succession and fire — Which recovery is secondary succession?
options: Colonisation of bare new rock without soil
Recolonisation after fire with soil retained
questions.explanation: Remaining soil and biological remnants distinguish secondary succession from primary establishment.

questions.prompt: Habitats, ecological niches and species interactions — What defines a keystone species?
questions.explanation: Keystone effects are large relative to abundance and may involve cascades through community interactions.

questions.prompt: Ecological fieldwork, data and scientific inquiry — Which method best describes sampling at regular distances along a gradient?
questions.explanation: Systematic intervals along transects reveal changes across a gradient, ideally with independent transects.

questions.prompt: Population dynamics, carrying capacity, succession and fire — What can change carrying capacity?
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is conditional on habitat and resources rather than a permanent species constant.

questions.prompt: Population dynamics, carrying capacity, succession and fire — What is characteristic of the simple logistic model?
questions.explanation: Density-related limits produce an S-shaped approach to carrying capacity under simplified conditions.

questions.prompt: Population dynamics, carrying capacity, succession and fire — Which calculation gives population change?
questions.explanation: Population gains and losses must have appropriate signs over the same interval.

questions.prompt: Population dynamics, carrying capacity, succession and fire — Why can equal population counts imply different futures?
questions.explanation: Composition, reproductive timing and survival matter; total size alone does not predict future change.

questions.prompt: Ecological fieldwork, data and scientific inquiry — What most reduces deliberate quadrat-location bias?
options: Random coordinates within a suitable frame
questions.explanation: Random placement reduces selection bias, but the sampling frame must still include relevant habitats.

questions.prompt: Habitats, ecological niches and species interactions — Which sign pair represents parasitism for parasite then host?
questions.explanation: The parasite gains a resource while the host incurs a cost; mutualism benefits both.

questions.prompt: Habitats, ecological niches and species interactions — How can resource partitioning reduce competition?
options: By reducing overlap in resource use
questions.explanation: Different times, places or resources can reduce direct competition while not eliminating all ecological limits.

questions.prompt: Habitats, ecological niches and species interactions — What can restrict a realised niche relative to a fundamental niche?
options: The printed width of a tree
questions.explanation: Biotic interactions such as competitors can prevent occupation of otherwise physiologically suitable conditions.

questions.prompt: Human impacts, conservation and evaluating management — Why is a seed bank insufficient alone?
options: It does not preserve the whole habitat and interactions
questions.explanation: Ex situ storage complements habitat management and cannot by itself maintain all ecosystem processes or restore lost variation.

questions.prompt: Human impacts, conservation and evaluating management — How can clearing contribute to dryland salinity?
options: Reduced deep-rooted uptake permits groundwater rise
questions.explanation: Hydrological changes can bring saline water toward the surface and concentrate salts through evaporation.

bio11-cells.title: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy
bio11-cells.unit: Unit 2 – From single cells to multicellular organisms
bio11-cells.parent: Unit 2 – From single cells to multicellular organisms
bio11-cells.coverage: Lesson concept checks followed by related subject revision.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — What primarily distinguishes typical eukaryotic from prokaryotic organisation?
options: An enclosed nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
questions.explanation: Both cell types share DNA, ribosomes, cytoplasm and membranes, but typical eukaryotes have compartmentalised organelles.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — Where are polypeptides assembled?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate mRNA using amino acids; Golgi and ER have subsequent processing/transport roles.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — Which plant-cell claim is accurate?
options: Roots make all sugar using darkness
Many root cells lack chloroplasts but respire
questions.explanation: Plant-cell structures vary with specialisation, and roots often receive organic compounds from sources.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — A 30 mm image represents a 10 μm object. What is magnification?
questions.explanation: Convert 30 mm to 30,000 μm then divide by 10 μm to obtain 3,000×.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — What does higher resolution permit?
questions.explanation: Resolution concerns detail separation, while magnification concerns image size.

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis, cellular respiration and ATP — Where does glycolysis occur in a typical eukaryotic cell?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is cytosolic, while later aerobic stages involve mitochondrial matrix and inner membrane.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — With other conditions fixed, higher humidity usually does what?
options: Reduces vapour gradient and water loss
questions.explanation: Higher external humidity lowers the diffusion gradient, although stomatal/environmental interactions can modify real responses.

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis, cellular respiration and ATP — Where does carbon fixation occur in a chloroplast?
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle uses CO₂ and products of light reactions in the chloroplast stroma.

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis, cellular respiration and ATP — What does fermentation permit?
questions.explanation: Regenerating carriers permits continued glycolysis; fermentation does not deliver the full aerobic ATP yield.

questions.prompt: Membranes, diffusion, osmosis and active transport — What causes plasmolysis in a suitable plant cell?
questions.explanation: Water loss shrinks the protoplast away from the relatively rigid wall under an appropriate external water potential.

questions.prompt: Biological molecules, metabolism and enzyme action — Why does substrate-dependent rate plateau?
questions.explanation: At high substrate, active sites are occupied much of the time, limiting further rate increase at fixed enzyme concentration.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — What do source and sink describe?
questions.explanation: Sources and sinks depend on developmental state and activity, so phloem direction is not universally downward.

questions.prompt: Biological molecules, metabolism and enzyme action — How does cooling usually differ from severe heating?
options: It slows encounters without necessarily denaturing
It always destroys every peptide bond
questions.explanation: Low temperature commonly reduces kinetic activity reversibly; sufficiently high heat can disrupt functional conformation.

questions.prompt: Animal exchange, digestion, transport and excretion — How does countercurrent exchange help?
options: It maintains a gradient along the surface
questions.explanation: Opposing flows preserve a favourable concentration gradient across much of the exchange region.

questions.prompt: Biological molecules, metabolism and enzyme action — What does an enzyme lower?
questions.explanation: Catalysis changes the reaction pathway/barrier rather than the overall energy difference or stoichiometry.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — What is a potometer’s direct measurement?
questions.explanation: Water uptake approximates transpiration but differs because storage, growth and leaks can affect measured flow.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — What supplies the principal pull in transpiration-driven xylem flow?
questions.explanation: Leaf evaporation creates tension transmitted through cohesive water columns; xylem is not an ATP water pump.

questions.prompt: Animal exchange, digestion, transport and excretion — Which structure is central to insect gas delivery?
questions.explanation: Tracheal tubes convey air toward tissues in the standard insect model, rather than relying primarily on blood for oxygen delivery.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — Which conducting tissue is usually dead at maturity?
questions.explanation: Xylem conducting elements are lignified and dead at maturity, while phloem relies on living sieve elements and companion cells.

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis, cellular respiration and ATP — What does zero net CO₂ exchange in light necessarily establish?
options: Uptake and release are balanced at that measurement
questions.explanation: Net exchange can be zero when opposing processes balance; it does not independently establish that both rates are zero.

bio11-membranes.coverage: Lesson concept checks followed by related subject revision.

questions.prompt: Membranes, diffusion, osmosis and active transport — Which phospholipid arrangement is appropriate?
options: A solid wall with no proteins
questions.explanation: Amphipathic phospholipids form a bilayer with hydrophobic tails sheltered from aqueous fluids.

questions.prompt: Membranes, diffusion, osmosis and active transport — What is facilitated diffusion?
questions.explanation: Channels/carriers assist passive movement; protein involvement alone does not make transport active.

questions.prompt: Membranes, diffusion, osmosis and active transport — What causes plasmolysis in a suitable plant cell?
questions.explanation: Water loss shrinks the protoplast away from the relatively rigid wall under an appropriate external water potential.

questions.prompt: Membranes, diffusion, osmosis and active transport — For a cube of side 2, what is SA:V?
questions.explanation: SA=6×4=24 and V=8, giving ratio 3:1; SA:V declines with increasing side length.

questions.prompt: Membranes, diffusion, osmosis and active transport — Which process releases large secreted cargo through vesicle fusion?
questions.explanation: Exocytosis merges a vesicle membrane with the cell membrane and releases its contents outside.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — Which plant-cell claim is accurate?
options: Roots make all sugar using darkness
Many root cells lack chloroplasts but respire
questions.explanation: Plant-cell structures vary with specialisation, and roots often receive organic compounds from sources.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — What do source and sink describe?
questions.explanation: Sources and sinks depend on developmental state and activity, so phloem direction is not universally downward.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — What is a potometer’s direct measurement?
questions.explanation: Water uptake approximates transpiration but differs because storage, growth and leaks can affect measured flow.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — What supplies the principal pull in transpiration-driven xylem flow?
questions.explanation: Leaf evaporation creates tension transmitted through cohesive water columns; xylem is not an ATP water pump.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — Which conducting tissue is usually dead at maturity?
questions.explanation: Xylem conducting elements are lignified and dead at maturity, while phloem relies on living sieve elements and companion cells.

questions.prompt: Plant gas exchange, xylem, phloem and transport investigations — With other conditions fixed, higher humidity usually does what?
options: Reduces vapour gradient and water loss
questions.explanation: Higher external humidity lowers the diffusion gradient, although stomatal/environmental interactions can modify real responses.

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis, cellular respiration and ATP — Where does glycolysis occur in a typical eukaryotic cell?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is cytosolic, while later aerobic stages involve mitochondrial matrix and inner membrane.

questions.prompt: Animal exchange, digestion, transport and excretion — What defines an artery?
options: Blood flows away from the heart
questions.explanation: Direction relative to the heart defines artery/vein; pulmonary arteries demonstrate the oxygen-content exception.

questions.prompt: Animal exchange, digestion, transport and excretion — Which waste generally requires least water for elimination?
questions.explanation: Uric-acid elimination conserves water but costs relatively more energy to synthesise, with species-specific details.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — A 30 mm image represents a 10 μm object. What is magnification?
questions.explanation: Convert 30 mm to 30,000 μm then divide by 10 μm to obtain 3,000×.

questions.prompt: Animal exchange, digestion, transport and excretion — How does countercurrent exchange help?
options: It maintains a gradient along the surface
questions.explanation: Opposing flows preserve a favourable concentration gradient across much of the exchange region.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — What does higher resolution permit?
questions.explanation: Resolution concerns detail separation, while magnification concerns image size.

questions.prompt: Animal exchange, digestion, transport and excretion — Which removal is excretion?
options: Only undigested food leaving the gut
questions.explanation: Excretion removes metabolic wastes; egestion removes undigested gut contents.

questions.prompt: Animal exchange, digestion, transport and excretion — Which structure is central to insect gas delivery?
questions.explanation: Tracheal tubes convey air toward tissues in the standard insect model, rather than relying primarily on blood for oxygen delivery.

questions.prompt: Cell structure, organelles and microscopy — Where are polypeptides assembled?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate mRNA using amino acids; Golgi and ER have subsequent processing/transport roles.

questions.prompt: Biological molecules, metabolism and enzyme action — What does an enzyme lower?
questions.explanation: Catalysis changes the reaction pathway/barrier rather than the overall energy difference or stoichiometry.

questions.prompt: Biological molecules, metabolism and enzyme action — What best describes induced fit?
questions.explanation: Induced fit represents flexible enzyme–substrate interaction and positioning supporting catalysis.

questions.prompt: Biological molecules, metabolism and enzyme action — Why does substrate-dependent rate plateau?
questions.explanation: At high substrate, active sites are occupied much of the time, limiting further rate increase at fixed enzyme concentration.

questions.prompt: Biological molecules, metabolism and enzyme action — What links amino acids in a protein backbone?
options: Only hydrogen bonds between DNA bases
questions.explanation: Peptide bonds join amino acids, while folding involves additional interactions that may be altered by denaturation.

questions.prompt: Biological molecules, metabolism and enzyme action — How does cooling usually differ from severe heating?
options: It slows encounters without necessarily denaturing
It always destroys every peptide bond
questions.explanation: Low temperature commonly reduces kinetic activity reversibly; sufficiently high heat can disrupt functional conformation.
